title: Coming home
hook: he returns to Kapilavatthu; young Rahula asks for his inheritance and is given the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputta and Moggallana: two friends, one pact, and Assaji's four-line verse. Your line was one verse was enough. Who got your good line? Day sixty-nine.

Going home after a long time away is its own kind of nervous. The streets look smaller. Everyone knows the old you. Remember the night Siddhartha left Kapilavatthu, the palace, his wife Yasodhara asleep, their newborn son Rahula beside her. He didn't wake them. Now, years later, word reaches his father, King Suddhodana, that his son has become a famous teacher. The king sends messengers begging him to visit. And he comes. But not the way a prince comes home. He walks into his hometown with a crowd of monks, and in the morning he does what monks do. He goes from house to house along the streets, with a bowl, asking for food.
screen: `THE STREETS LOOK SMALLER.` → `THE KING SENDS FOR HIM.` → `A PRINCE WITH A BOWL.`

segments.voice: Later tradition fills in the scene. The king is mortified. My son, begging, in my own city? Our family has never done this. The Buddha answers that his family now is the line of Buddhas before him, and this is their custom. Then comes the moment the old monastic texts do record. Rahula is about seven now. His mother, Yasodhara, sends him to his father with a message. Go and ask him for your inheritance. So a small boy walks up to the teacher everyone's talking about, stands close, and the texts say he told him, pleasant is your shadow, monk. Then, when the Buddha gets up and walks away, Rahula follows him, saying: give me my inheritance, monk. Give me my inheritance. And here's the Buddha's answer. He doesn't hand over land, or gold, or a crown. He turns to Sariputta, the wise friend from yesterday, and asks him to ordain the boy. Rahula becomes the first novice, a young monk in training. The reasoning, as the commentaries tell it: the wealth he's asking for brings trouble and ends. I'll give him an inheritance that doesn't. The texts are honest that this hurt. King Suddhodana, who had already lost his son to the road, now loses his grandson too. He goes to the Buddha and says: when my son left, it was pain. When his son left, it was pain again. Please, don't let children be ordained without their parents' permission. And the Buddha agrees, and makes it a rule. Buddhist monasteries still keep it: a child needs a parent's consent. So one family's grief became a kindness for every family after.
screen: `A PRINCE WITH A BOWL.` · `GIVE ME MY INHERITANCE.` · `THE BOY IS GIVEN THE TEACHING.` · `A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.` · then, large: `THE REAL INHERITANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone something that lasts. Settle and breathe. Think of what you've inherited that wasn't money. A way your grandmother laughed. How your father fixed things. A saying, a recipe, a habit of patience. Let one come to mind, and feel it for a moment. Then think of someone younger, a child, a niece, a new coworker. What's one thing you could pass on to them that no one could take away? The bell holds the time.
Coming home. The Buddha returns to Kapilavatthu with a bowl, and his son Rahula, asking for an inheritance, is given the teaching.
Your line: the real inheritance. Today, pass on one thing that can't be bought, a skill, a story, a kindness, to someone who'll outlast you. Day sixty-nine.

howItsDone: In many Theravada countries boys ordain for a time as novices, following Rahula as the first, and monasteries require parents' permission before a child is ordained, a rule traced to King Suddhodana's request.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. your seven-year-old son follows you, asking over and over for his inheritance. what do you give him?
options: a share of the palace and land.
a kind word, and send him home.
the teaching: he's ordained as a novice.
fork.reveal: he asks Sariputta to ordain the boy. and when the grandfather grieves, he makes a rule that parents must consent.

original.note: Pali: inheritance, heritage. What Rahula asked for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a father who walked out coming back to make amends.
what it means: a son asks for his inheritance and is given the teaching, and a grandfather's grief becomes a rule that protects families.

what a scholar hears: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.54: 'give me my inheritance, samana' (dayajjam me samana dehi); the parental-consent rule for ordination; the alms-round scene and 'custom of the Buddhas' come from later commentary.

sources.ref: Jataka Nidanakatha; Dhammapada commentary (return to Kapilavatthu)

notes: The alms-round scene and the 'lineage of Buddhas' answer come from commentarial accounts; the script marks them 'later tradition'. The Rahula scene and Suddhodana's request are in Mahavagga 1.54.
Rahula's age of seven follows commentarial tradition; confirm.
'Pleasant is your shadow, monk' (sukha te samana chaya) paraphrased from Mv 1.54; confirm.
'Rahula becomes the first novice' (samanera): standard; confirm.
The commentarial reasoning ('wealth that brings trouble... an inheritance that doesn't', the sevenfold noble wealth) is paraphrased and attributed to the commentaries.
